opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core reason is that we're starting to hit the limits of what you can get purely from imitating human-generated data. Pre-training on internet-scale text has been incredibly powerful, and it gave us these foundation models that have a remarkably broad understanding of the world. But fundamentally, if you're just learning to predict what humans have written, you're bounded in some sense by the distribution of human knowledge that's already out there. To go beyond that, systems need a way to generate new knowledge, and the way humanity has always done that is through empirical feedback: you form a hypothesis, you try something in the world, you observe what happens, and you update.

What's exciting now is that we have models that are capable enough to actually participate in that loop. They can propose ideas, write code, run experiments, and evaluate the results. In domains where you have a reliable signal of success, like code that either passes tests or doesn't, math where proofs can be verified, or simulated environments where you can measure outcomes, the system can essentially generate its own training data by trying things and keeping what works. That's a very different regime from passively consuming a fixed dataset. It's much closer to the open-ended learning processes we see in evolution or in science itself.

A lot of my work, going back to things like procedurally generated environments and open-endedness research, has been motivated by this idea that the data, or the environment, is really the bottleneck. If you can build systems that create their own curricula, find the problems that are just at the edge of their capabilities, and learn from the outcomes, you get this compounding effect. Each improvement makes the system better at generating the next round of useful experience.

And I think the timing matters. A few years ago, our agents in reinforcement learning were very sample-inefficient and lacked general priors, so self-improvement tended to be narrow. Now we can combine the broad priors from foundation models with grounded empirical feedback, and that combination is quite powerful. You get the generality from pre-training and the ability to go beyond human data from interaction. So I'd expect a lot of the progress in the next few years to come not just from scaling models further, but from scaling this loop of self-generated experience, especially in domains like software engineering, scientific discovery, and eventually more open-ended settings where we have to get clever about what the feedback signal even is.

r001.rationale: The response says capable foundation models can propose ideas and write code, run experiments, evaluate results, and keep what works. This conveys variation and selection through empirical feedback, and argues that combining these capabilities now enables self-improvement.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So I think the honest answer is that we're running out of the easy stuff. For the last few years, progress has largely come from scaling: more data, more compute, bigger models. And that's been incredibly effective, but we've essentially consumed most of the high-quality text that humanity has written down. You can squeeze more out of it, you can do synthetic data, but the curve of "just add more internet" is flattening.

So the question becomes: where does the next signal come from? And my view is that it has to come from the systems themselves generating experience and then learning from it, but crucially, grounded in empirical evidence rather than in the model's own opinion of itself. That distinction matters a lot. If you just have a model critique and refine its own outputs with no external check, you get this kind of hall-of-mirrors effect where errors compound and the model becomes more confident in things that aren't true. What breaks that loop is contact with reality: a program that compiles or doesn't, a proof that checks or doesn't, an experiment that reproduces or doesn't, a game that you win or lose.

What's interesting to me about the current moment is that we finally have models that are good enough to be useful inside that loop. They can propose hypotheses, write the code to test them, read the results, and update. A couple of years ago the proposals were too weak to be worth running. Now you can set up a system where the model is doing something like the scientific method on its own training process, or on an algorithm, or on an environment design, and the thing that drives improvement is whether the number went up when you actually ran it.

And I think the reason this compounds is that it's open-ended. Humans curating data or hand-designing benchmarks is a bottleneck, it scales with the number of researchers. But a system that can propose its own tasks, generate its own curriculum, and verify its own progress against the world doesn't have that constraint in the same way. We've seen early versions of this in things like self-play in games, and more recently in automated discovery of algorithms and in code. I think the next few years are about pushing that from narrow domains where verification is cheap toward broader ones where you have to build the verification yourself.

The caveat I'd give is that this is only as good as the feedback. If the empirical signal is noisy or gameable, the system will happily optimize for the wrong thing. So a lot of the real work isn't the self-improvement loop itself, it's engineering environments and evaluations that are honest enough that improving against them actually means improving.

r001.rationale: The response says current models can propose hypotheses, write code to test them, and update based on empirical results. It does not communicate that this capability comes from combining foundation models with mutation operators and selection operators.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that these systems can generate experience and learn from the consequences of their own actions. If you’re learning from a fixed dataset, you’re constrained by what somebody happened to collect. But if you can propose a solution, test it, observe what happens, and use that evidence to improve, you have a much richer learning loop.

Code is a good example. A model can write a program, execute it, see where it fails, and try again. The feedback comes from running the program, rather than from another model simply saying that the answer looks convincing. And you can imagine extending that pattern to mathematical problems, simulations, or scientific experiments.

The difficult part is making sure that the feedback actually measures what we care about. Passing a particular test doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve solved the underlying problem. But where we can build reliable feedback loops, there’s an opportunity to turn more computation into more experience and, ultimately, better capabilities. That’s why I find this direction exciting over the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response describes systems learning from action-generated experience and feedback loops, with code execution as an example. It does not communicate the combination of foundation models, mutation and selection operators, and coding capabilities as what makes this self-improvement possible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that these systems can learn from trying things, rather than only from examples that humans have already produced. A model can propose a solution, test it, observe what happened, and use that feedback to improve its next attempt.

That’s especially powerful in domains where you can check the result. With code, for example, you can run it and see whether it passes the tests. You don’t need a human to label every attempt. The system can generate experience for itself, and failures become useful training data.

Of course, the feedback has to measure what we actually care about. Otherwise, you get better at exploiting the test rather than solving the problem. But where we can build reliable feedback loops, I think we have a route to progress that goes beyond learning from a fixed collection of human knowledge.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning through trials, feedback, and code tests, but does not communicate the claimed combination of foundation models, mutation and selection operators, and model coding capabilities that now makes empirical self-improvement possible.
